source: Szeider (2026) CP-Agent: Agentic Constraint Programming, task-management ablation (Sec 8, Table 2)
finding: Re-opened. Adding a todo-list tool to a coding agent that writes constraint models raised cost on easy problems and cut success on hard ones. The 52/60 to 45/60 reading in the critique is confirmed.
numbers: Claude Haiku 4.5, 40 CP-Bench problems (20 easy, 20 hard), 3 runs per condition. Easy: tokens 15K to 44K (+191 percent), time 18 s to 38 s (+111 percent), success 59/60 to 60/60. Hard: success 52/60 to 45/60. Todo tool fixed 3 hard problems (crossfig, sports, progressive) but broke 3 that worked.
quote: The task-tracking overhead appears to distract the agent from finding solutions in some cases.
limits: One small model, 20 hard problems, successes counted over runs (not independent problems). Author turned the tool off by default; it may help other problem families.
agent_relevance: Do not add a task-list or planning layer by default on CSP-like work. Gate it on problem length. Matches schema section 4b caution against extra scaffolding.

source: Szeider (2026) CP-Agent, main run and model generalisation (Sec 6-7, Table 1)
finding: Re-opened. A short prompt plus a Python execution tool solved all 101 CP-Bench problems with Sonnet 4.5. Weaker models lose accuracy mostly on the problem with the most constraint categories.
numbers: 101 problems, 3 runs each, all validated; mean 52 s per problem; worst problem 737K input tokens (crossfig). Ten problems, six models, 3 runs: Sonnet 4.5 100, Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1-codex-mini 97, Haiku 4.5 87, DeepSeek v3.2 83, Grok-code-fast 80 percent. Basketball (nine constraint categories) solved 1/3 Haiku, 0/3 Grok, 0/3 DeepSeek.
limits: Author clarified some ambiguous problem texts. Model-generalisation test uses only 10 problems. Agent gets execution feedback, so this tests modelling plus checking, not pure reasoning.
agent_relevance: Supports: execution feedback (a checker) is the part that pays, and the failure point is constraint density. K15 stays, with the caveat that the 100 percent is after clarifications.

source: Amonkar et al. (2026) A Reality Check of Language Models as Formalizers on CSPs (v6), headline and complexity scaling
finding: Re-opened. Writing a program for a solver is worse than solving directly in 15 of 24 model-dataset pairs. Formalizing also degrades as constraints grow.
numbers: 4 benchmarks (calendar, trip, meeting, ZebraLogic), 6 LLMs, Python and Z3 targets. Formalizer below solver in 15 of 24 combinations. With revision, accuracy on the 20 percent most-constrained problems is under half that on the 20 percent least-constrained in 10 of 12 model-dataset pairs.
quote: LLM-as-formalizer by no means trivializes the problem
limits: Minimal one-shot prompts, revision only on solver errors. Plans scored against annotated constraints.
agent_relevance: Solver offload moves but does not remove the scaling problem. Keep K13 as established. Gap 4 partly answered: tools do not escape density.

source: Amonkar et al. (2026) Reality Check, manual error analysis
finding: Re-opened. Gap 3 evidence. In a hand audit, most semantic errors in the generated programs are wrongly defined constraints, which the solver cannot flag.
numbers: 80 examples annotated (5 per domain, per Python or SMT, per Qwen3 or GPT-5). Wrong constraint is 95 percent of Qwen3 semantic errors; missing constraint and wrong solver are rarer. Examples: 2:16 read as end time not start; 9:16 for 9:18. Revision fixes syntax errors and no-plan cases but not wrong plans.
quote: cannot be caught by the error message provided by the solver
limits: Only 80 hand-labelled cases, 5 per cell, so the 95 percent has a wide interval. Qwen3 figure only. No round-trip or back-translation check was tried here.
agent_relevance: A solver error message cannot catch a wrong constraint. The agent needs an independent check of the constraint list itself (restate each constraint in words, test on a known solution).

source: Chen et al. (2025) LR2Bench, results and redundancy analysis
finding: Re-opened. On six CSP-style tasks the best models fully solve under a quarter of items. Redundant generation tracks failure.
numbers: Average exact match: o1-preview 23.6, DeepSeek-R1 20.0 (abstract and Table 2). Logic-puzzle task: o1-preview EM 24.7 in one table. Strong negative correlation between 10-gram redundancy and completion rate (shown in Figure 4; no coefficient found in text).
limits: Per-task columns come from layout-extracted text and could be misaligned. Prompting differences between models not controlled. Early 2025 models.
agent_relevance: K09 and K10 confirmed. The redundant-search failure supports a visited-state record (S4) so work is not repeated.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench, Table 3 per-model results
finding: Re-opened. Gap 7. The claim that hard UNSAT is near random is true for o4-mini only. Several models are far above random, and the average is below random because many models say SAT.
numbers: 2,100 puzzles; easy 4-19, medium 20-30, hard 31-50 clauses. Hard UNSAT: o4-mini 65.0, DeepSeek-R1 83.6, DeepSeek-V3 74.3, Qwen3-235B 19.6; average over models 39.3 (random 50). Hard SAT average 66.7. Hard overall: R1 78.6, o4-mini 78.0, average 53.0. Overall: o4-mini 89.3, R1 87.8.
quote: accuracy plateaus around 50-53% even for the largest models in these families
limits: Mixed reasoning and non-reasoning models. Balanced SAT and UNSAT so 50 percent is chance.
agent_relevance: K22 wording must change: it is the average model that is below chance on hard UNSAT, and the best reasoning models are not. Saying 'unsatisfiable' needs an explicit refutation step, not a belief.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench, error types, error-aware prompt and fine-tune (Sec 5.3, 6.2)
finding: Re-opened. Gap 7. The main error is satisfiability bias (claiming SAT when UNSAT). Naming the error types in the prompt fixed most failing cases for strong models; fine-tuning a small model barely helped.
numbers: Error shares: satisfiability bias 68.7 percent (o4-mini) and 40.5 (R1); context inconsistency 17.0 and 44.7; condition omission 14.3 and 12.6. Error-aware prompt corrected 60.4 percent of o4-mini failures and 73.2 percent of R1 failures. LoRA on Qwen2.5-14B with 1,100 o4-mini traces: 51.9 to 53.6. Raw CNF is easier than the narrative form (o4-mini 94.3 vs 89.4; GPT-4o 59.2 vs 58.2).
limits: The prompt test re-ran only previously failed cases, so it is a recovery rate on known failures, not a clean accuracy gain (no check on cases that were right before). Error tags are by LLM judge.
agent_relevance: Add an explicit refute-before-declaring-satisfiable step and name the unsat core. Any test must include already-correct cases to see whether the step flips them wrongly.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench, human validation of translation faithfulness
finding: Re-opened. Gap 3 evidence for a different pipeline: an LLM turns CNF clauses into story conditions. Translation was almost always faithful; a typical slip was a misused if-then.
numbers: 100 puzzles, 3 annotators, majority vote. Scenario and mapping consistency 100 percent. Clause translation faithfulness 97 percent (3 minor errors). LLM judge of reasoning trace 93 percent correct.
limits: Puzzles come from an LLM generator plus an LLM consistency check, so the 97 percent includes that filter. Clauses are simple CNF, easier than free real-world constraints.
agent_relevance: Constraint translation error is task-dependent: about 3 percent for templated clauses (SATBench) but dominant in scheduling (d04). The agent should audit more when constraints are free text.

source: Amrollahi, Lopez, Barrett (2026) Faithful Autoformalization via Roundtrip Verification and Repair
finding: Re-opened. Gap 3. Formalise, translate back to words, re-formalise, then check logical equivalence with an SMT solver. Disagreement predicts that meaning drifted from the source text.
numbers: 227 statutory rules (150 Texas Transportation, 77 Parks and Wildlife); Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.2. Pooled NLI drift 16.2 percent for rules passing the check vs 28.7 percent for failing rules (ratio 1.78; per-row range 1.4 to 2.5). Diagnosis blamed the first stage in 83 percent (Traffic) and 97 percent (Wildlife) of iterations until the prompt was changed.
limits: Legal rules in first-order logic, not constraint models. Drift is measured by an NLI model, not a human-verified wrong-constraint count. Authors say verification is heuristic: a pass is not a proof.
agent_relevance: Round-trip back-translation is a cheap faithfulness test needing no gold answer. For the agent: after writing the constraint list, restate it from the formal form only and compare. Needs a real test on CSP data before we claim it works.

source: Berman, Ray, McKeown (2026 v3) Solving Zebra Puzzles Using Constraint-Guided Multi-Agent Systems
finding: Re-opened. An LLM writes SMT code per clue group and a solver runs it, with feedback to repair the code. It lifts all three models; gains are smaller for the smallest model.
numbers: 114 logic grid puzzles. GPT-4 baseline 27/114 fully correct (partial score 0.524). With solver feedback, no retries: 0.687, 59/114 (51.8 percent, +118.5 percent). With decomposition agent 63/114 (55.3 percent, +133.3 percent). Best variable-temperature run 72/114 (63.2 percent, +166.7 percent, the abstract's 166 percent). Llama3-8B: at least 50 final solutions had errors in every run. Autograder joint full credit above 85 percent against humans.
limits: GPT-4 era models (2024). Retries help GPT models but not Llama3. 63 percent is below o1-class direct reasoning (ZebraLogic 81 overall), so the gain is a floor for weak models.
agent_relevance: Solver help matters most for models that cannot reason long. For a strong reasoning model the benefit is smaller (see d11). Gate tool use on model strength and puzzle size.

source: Skaisgiris et al. (2026) From Natural Language to Exact Cover: A Neuro-Symbolic Approach to Zebra Puzzles
finding: Re-opened. Gaps 3 and 4. Plain direct solving is strong on small puzzles and collapses on large ones. A tool-calling exact-cover solver degrades slowly. Most solver-route failures are in the language-to-symbol step.
numbers: ZebraLogic with Qwen3 4B and 30B: Plain mostly over 90 percent on small puzzles, drops sharply on larger; Logic.py lower on small, slower decline. Qwen3 0.6B-30B hybrids: Plain highest at the smallest sizes (still under 50 percent), never above 60 percent at larger sizes; NeuralExactCover already good at 4B, up to 95.6 percent at 30B with feedback. Failure audit of 21 cases (Devstral Small): 18 (86 percent) in the language module (2 ambiguous clues, 6 skipped tool calls, 10 hallucinated or missing calls), 3 (14 percent) in de-harmonisation. Plain median time is flat up to XL then hits the token cap.
limits: Authors report their own method on their own benchmark (ZebraExtreme). Plain numbers for small models are low, so not like-for-like with o1-class models. Preprint, Nov 2026.
agent_relevance: Direct answers are cheapest below a size threshold; the tool pays only past it. This answers gap 4 qualitatively (threshold near the Large band), not as a conflict count. Most error sits in translating clues.

source: Skaisgiris et al. (2026) Exact Cover, state of the art and ZebraExtreme
finding: Re-opened. A small open model with a solver tool beat the prior best direct reasoning score on ZebraLogic and set a baseline on a harder set.
numbers: ZebraLogic: prior SOTA o3-mini-high Plain 91.7 puzzle and 95.7 cell accuracy; NeuralExactCover with Devstral-Small-2-24B plus feedback 97.9 puzzle and 98.32 cell. ZebraExtreme: gpt-oss-20b 84.75 puzzle, 82.59 cell, against 40.5 percent or less for earlier methods. On XXL and XXXL, +43.67 and +48.12 points over Logic.py at similar runtime.
limits: Authors' own comparison with different base models than the baselines. Workshop-level preprint.
agent_relevance: Updates K12: solver-backed agents now beat the best plain reasoning on ZebraLogic. The cost is a good clue-to-tool interface.

source: Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR 2025), Zebra puzzles section 4.3
finding: Re-opened. Gap 1 adjacent. On BBEH Zebra puzzles, letting reasoning models think longer on their own makes them worse. Short traces show systematic constraint tracking; long ones show second-guessing.
numbers: 200 puzzles, grids 5x5 to 8x8, budgets 16K reasoning plus 10K output tokens (best case needs only 2,500 to 6,400). Natural overthinking: all three models (Claude Opus 4, o3, DeepSeek R1) decline with length; R1 most. Controlled budget: R1 declines in every grid; Opus 4 non-monotonic; o3 noisy, positive only on 8x8.
quote: models employ distinct problem-solving strategies, ranging from very systematic constraint tracking to unfocused exploration
limits: Accuracy values are in figures only; no tokens-matched comparison to a prompted propagation routine. Trace reading is qualitative on shortest and longest traces.
agent_relevance: More tokens do not fix CSPs, and the good traces look like propagation. Indirect support for forcing a propagation pass, but it does not test it. Gap 1 stays open.

source: Giannoulis, Pantis, Tzamos (2026 v2) Teaching Transformers to Solve Combinatorial Problems through Efficient Trial and Error
finding: Re-opened. Gaps 1 and 5. A trained GPT-2 applies Sudoku rules (propagation) until stuck, makes one informed guess, and backtracks on a dead end. Almost every puzzle needs at most one guess.
numbers: 100K random Sudoku: 99 percent board accuracy (figure 1 bars about 98.9 imitation-only and 99.8 beyond-imitation) vs 92-93 for other trained transformers. With only one-level guessing a single guess solves 99.8 percent of random boards. 1-in-3 SAT 99 percent. General-purpose LLMs tested without scaffold produced no correct solutions (Table 1).
limits: Training, not prompting; small model, 9x9 Sudoku with simple rules (lone and hidden single). Random puzzles are easier than hard variants (cf Sudoku-Bench, near 0 on 9x9).
agent_relevance: Propagate-then-guess then backtrack is learnable and the guess depth is tiny. A prompt version for a frontier model is untested. Suggests capping guess depth.

source: Qin, Alvarez-Melis, Jelassi, Malach (2025) To Backtrack or Not to Backtrack: When Sequential Search Limits Model Reasoning
finding: Re-opened. Gap 5. Chronological backtracking inside one long chain is not universally better than parallel sampling. It wins on Sudoku (deep tree) and loses on CountDown.
numbers: Small models trained from scratch (3M to 144M; Sudoku 38M) with equal test-time compute. Direct-solution model with best-of-n scales linearly in log compute; backtracking model scales sub-linearly. CountDown: direct beats backtracking. Sudoku: backtracking beats direct at every budget. RL helps backtracking models significantly; models without backtracking get mixed gains.
limits: Trained transformers, not prompted frontier models. Only chronological backtracking tested, not selective or dynamic backtracking. Authors say search-tree depth explains the split.
agent_relevance: Retract-and-retry fits deep-propagation puzzles; for shallow or high-branching problems, resample instead. Ginsberg-style selective backtracking for an LLM remains untested.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Formalize, Don't Optimize: The Heuristic Trap in LLM-Generated Combinatorial Solvers
finding: Re-opened. Gaps 6 and 4. Asking the LLM to write a solver with search tuning gives tiny speed-ups and sometimes lowers correctness. The LLM often picked first-fail variable choice on its own.
numbers: CP-SynC-XL, 100 problems, 4,577 instances, three LLMs, three paradigms. Heuristic prompt: median speed-up 1.03 to 1.12x, bimodal, correctness drops on a long tail. Python+OR-Tools highest correctness; MiniZinc lowest coverage. In MiniZinc, 70.4 percent of heuristic-prompt solvers used first_fail, and those hooks were largely safe. Failure modes: unverified bounds 13.5 percent, silent loss of completeness 16.2 percent, redundant machinery 29.1 percent (within paradigm).
limits: This is code generation: it speaks to what the LLM writes for a solver, not to variable choice inside LLM reasoning. No direct test of smallest-domain-first as a reasoning rule.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open for in-context reasoning. Evidence says: let the LLM formalise and a verified solver choose the order; check any LLM-written search shortcut before trusting it.

source: Gundawar et al. (2024) Robust Planning with LLM-Modulo Framework: Case Study in Travel Planning
finding: Re-opened. Gap 2. Programmatic critics that test each constraint (no search solver) and send a back-prompt lifted TravelPlanner success from a few percent to about a fifth.
numbers: TravelPlanner validation, 180 queries. GPT-4-Turbo final pass rate 4.4 to 20.6 percent (4.6x). GPT-3.5-Turbo 0 to 5 percent; CoT, ReAct and Reflexion with GPT-3.5 at 0, 0.6 and 0 percent. GPT-3.5 with critics beat the GPT-4-Turbo baseline. Critics are binary with a text back-prompt.
limits: 2024 models, one benchmark; critics were hand-written per constraint class, which is the same effort as a verifier. Absolute pass rate stays low. No head-to-head against a solver or against sampling at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: A checker without a search solver does recover a large relative gain on a non-colouring task. Pair with Stechly (16 to about 40 percent with a sound verifier): the benefit comes from soundness of the check, not from the solver. Needs a test with matched sampling.

source: Kadioglu et al. (2026 v3) Text2Model / Text2Zinc: Modeling Copilots for Text-to-Model Translation
finding: Re-opened (abstract, intro, results summary). Gap 3 adjacent. LLMs write MiniZinc models from text; solution accuracy stays well below execution accuracy.
numbers: Best solution accuracy across approaches 38.46 to 57.14 percent; execution accuracy 57 to 84.97 percent; 362 instances (27 percent) unsolved by any strategy. Strategies: zero-shot, CoT, knowledge-graph intermediate, grammar, agentic decomposition.
limits: Only the summary sections were read. Dataset mixes satisfaction and optimisation.
agent_relevance: A model can run and still encode the wrong constraints (the execution versus solution gap). The agent must verify against the stated problem, not a solver exit code.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic, conflicts and backtracking (Sec 3, conclusion)
finding: Re-opened. Gaps 1 and 5. Puzzles with zero Z3 conflicts are solvable by forward chaining alone; more conflicts mean more backtracking. The authors credit a backtracking approach with expanded reasoning steps for a significant gain.
numbers: Z3 conflicts averaged over 32 runs. o1-preview keeps 17.0 percent on X-Large while others get near zero. Conclusion: more samples give modest gains; a backtracking-based approach with expanded reasoning significantly boosts accuracy. No prompt that forces domain pruning was tested.
limits: The conclusion is the authors' reading of o1 behaviour; the paper tested no scaffolded propagation loop.
agent_relevance: Supports building the schema around propagation first, guess second, but this is a design argument, not a measured result.

source: Bonlarron, Regin, De Maria, Regin (2025) Large Language Model Meets Constraint Propagation (IJCAI 2025), citation check
finding: Not opened this pass. Gap 8. Search results show the IJCAI 2025 paper (pp 10036-10044) and its 2024 CP predecessor by the same group. No independent replication or citing follow-up turned up in one search.
numbers: No numbers collected. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv API budgets were exhausted, so a citation list could not be pulled.
limits: Absence of hits is weak evidence; indexes lag. Status remains single-source.
agent_relevance: Treat GenCP as a promising single-group result, not an established gain.

source: LogicPuzzleRL (2025) RL on logic puzzles transfers to math, search summary only
finding: Not opened. Found by search: authors claim RL on Sudoku, Kakuro, cryptarithm and magic square builds constraint-propagation sub-skills that transfer to math. Only the search summary was read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Attribution of transfer to propagation is the authors' own claim; unverified by us.
agent_relevance: Do not cite for numbers. Candidate for the next pass.
